title: Search Open Websites/Domains: Social Media
summary: This sub-technique narrows open website collection to social platforms, where employees describe their employer, tools, projects and daily frustrations in their own words. Adversaries passively harvest this material to build target lists with real names, job titles and reporting lines, then move to active variants such as fake recruiter profiles or interest groups that convince a target to volunteer further detail. The parent technique covers public web sources generally, whereas this one concentrates on the human and relationship layer that makes a pretext credible. Artefacts usually sit with the platform rather than the victim, so direct network telemetry is scarce. What defenders can work with is indirect: drive by visits from corporate addresses to profile pages, and later correlation with credential phishing or business email compromise attempts that reuse the harvested names. Detection therefore leans on brand monitoring for impersonation accounts, monitoring for fraudulent recruiter or supplier personas, and awareness training so staff recognise elicitation when it happens rather than reporting it weeks later.

beginner.definition: This is when an attacker gathers information from social media. They read posts, profiles, photos and comments about your organisation. They use those facts to learn who works where and what those people care about.
beginner.whyItMatters: Social posts give attackers real names, roles and personal interests. That makes a fake message far more believable. Staff also often accept contact from strangers who look like recruiters. The reading happens on the platform, so your own systems may record nothing at all.
howItWorks: The attacker searches social platforms for your organisation's name and its employees.
They read public profiles to learn job titles, teams and who reports to whom.
They study posts about projects, tools, travel and workplace events for useful detail.
They note interests and hobbies that can make a friendly message seem natural.
They may create a fake recruiter or supplier account to talk with staff directly.
They use the collected detail later in a targeted message that mentions real people and projects.
beginner.example: Think of a shared flat where everyone pins notes to the kitchen board about shifts, holidays and the new door code. A visitor waiting for a friend can read the whole board in two minutes. Nothing was forced open, but the visitor now knows when the flat is empty and how to get in.
takeaways: Every public profile is a small piece of a larger picture an attacker assembles.
Fake recruiter accounts are a common way to turn reading into conversation.
Report suspicious approaches early, because a conversation can be stopped but a harvested fact cannot.

objectives: Explain how this sub-technique differs from general open website searching.
Describe the employee details that social platforms expose to an attacker.
Recognise elicitation through fake profiles, groups or recruiter personas.
Describe the indirect signals available when collection happens off your network.
Apply practical social media hygiene advice for staff and teams.
